history.prompt: Low-angle architectural photograph of a modern data hall at blue hour; through a ground-floor glass curtain wall on the left, five identical server cabinets glow warm amber in a row—the five-node cluster—while a single cast-iron parking-style billing meter stands in the right foreground on a concrete plinth, its needle caught by the amber spill. 24mm architectural lens, deep focus, deep blue ambient light from the sky above, warm amber from the lit cabinets to the left, graphite, bone white, steel grey; glass and brushed steel and concrete; extreme asymmetric off-centre framing with building left and meter right; long-exposure calm, no people, no text, no logos, fine film grain.

history.prompt: Editorial paper collage laid on the dark plotting desk of a control room. Split-screen diptych: the left half holds one large cut-paper key silhouette in bone-white rag paper wearing a single blank copper price tag; the right half holds a fanned stack of six smaller duplicate cut-paper keys of the same shape, each copy wearing its own tiny blank copper tag, edges crisp, halftone newsprint texture across every layer. A vertical hand-torn seam of slate-grey paper divides the halves. Raking light from the left throws long physical cast shadows under each layer; visible paper fibre, bone white, slate grey and copper palette, generous negative space.

history.alt_text: A solid paper key beside the same key fanned into seven layered versions, lit from the upper left on a steel workbench.
history.caption: Both rate cards cover the same job — they just count different objects, and the object on the meter is the bill.
history.title: One Key, Seven Versions: The Object on the Meter

style_when: the article is a purely conceptual synthesis or policy dilemma where no physical facility, machine, or supply chain exists, and an elegant abstract paper silhouette states the idea. Never reach for paper collage when the story describes physical manufacturing, freight, energy, hardware, or heavy infrastructure — use cinematic still or telephoto industry instead
prompt: Cut-paper collage laid on a brushed-steel workbench in a dim server room. Left half: one solid bone-white paper key, cut crisp, lying flat on a graphite rag-paper sheet. Right half: the same key silhouette cut into seven thin layered paper copies, fanned like dealt cards, the seventh copy copper-toned, each layer casting its own long shadow. A hand-torn rag-paper seam with visible fibre divides the halves down the centre. One hard raking light from the upper left, low and directional, throws long crisp shadows to the lower right across the brushed steel. Palette of bone white, graphite and copper. Split-screen diptych with wide negative space above, fine matte grain.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, legible numbers, watermarks, printed or embossed lettering
rationale: This is a purely conceptual pricing dilemma with no facility or machine to photograph, which is exactly when the collage treatment earns its place. A key is the reader-legible silhouette of a secret, and the split-screen fan of seven layered copies states the article's spine — the crossover at seven live versions — without a word of text. The diptych also honors the two-scenario duality of the two vendors' meters.
cue: every live version of a secret
subject: a cut-paper key billed two ways — one solid key on the left, the same key fanned into seven layered versions on the right
core_thesis: A secrets manager bills the object you keep — AWS the secret, Google the live version — so rotation and rollback policy, not security doctrine, set the monthly bill.
core_conflict: Two rate cards for the same job that count different objects — what you store versus what you keep — so a rotation is free on one meter and a new billing line on the other, with the crossover at seven live versions.
composition: split-screen diptych: left half one solid key on a single sheet, right half the same key fanned into seven layered versions, a hand-torn paper seam dividing the halves, wide negative space above

review.reason: The visual contrast between a single key and multiple layered keys directly illustrates the concept of a single object versus multiple versions being billed.
